title: A day off
hookLine: Shabbat ends with a box of spices passed hand to hand; rest you don't have to earn
tomorrow: who stayed happy with one bowl of rice in a narrow lane?

lines: WHY A SWEET SMELL AT THE END?
cards: A Saturday with nothing on it, and by ten in the morning the work email is open again. Rest can feel like something you're supposed to earn first.
In Jewish homes, the day of rest, Shabbat, ends on Saturday night with a short ceremony called havdalah. A braided candle is lit. A cup of wine is blessed.
And then a small box of spices, cloves or cinnamon, goes around, and everyone breathes it in. Why spices? Why does the end of a rest day need a sweet smell?

teach.b: Start where the Bible starts the rest. Exodus says that in six days God made heaven and earth, "and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed." Even God, in the text, stops.
Then the Talmud adds a picture.

teach.h: AN EXTRA SOUL FOR THE DAY.
teach.b: Resh Lakish, one of its rabbis, said a person is given an extra soul on the eve of Shabbat, and at its end the extra soul is taken away.
Tradition explains the spices this way: a sweet smell to comfort you as that extra soul leaves. So the day of rest is something you'd miss, not something you got through.
And here's the part for anyone who can't stop checking email. The commandment says six days you shall labor and do all your work. All of it, in six days?

teach.h: RASHI: REGARD YOUR WORK AS DONE.
teach.b: Rashi, a medieval commentator, explains: when Shabbat comes, regard your work as done. Not finished; regarded as finished.
So in this Jewish teaching, rest isn't a prize at the end of a to-do list. It arrives on time, whether you're ready or not, and you're allowed to put the work down because the day says so.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat stop work from Friday sunset to Saturday night, then close it with havdalah: a braided candle, a blessing over wine, and spices passed around and smelled.

o: a prize you get after a very hard week
a day to catch up on chores and errands
a day when the work stops, finished or not

games.q: the end of the rest day: tap the pairs.
p: comfort as the extra soul leaves

s: in Jewish teaching, Shabbat is a reward for finishing the week's work
the popular idea of a day off. Rashi taught: when Shabbat comes, regard your work as done, finished or not.
at havdalah, spices are passed around and smelled
a sweet smell as the day of rest leaves.
in Exodus, God rests on the seventh day and is refreshed
Exodus 31:17: "and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed."

games.q: your coworker takes Sunday off, but first she works late Saturday night so she'll 'deserve' it. what fits Rashi's teaching?
o: stop when the day comes and treat the work as done, finished or not.
finish everything first; a day off only counts once it's earned.
skip the day off this week and take two in a row next week.
games.why: on 'six days you shall labor and do all your work', Rashi explains: when Shabbat comes, regard your work as done.

practice: Find something with a scent near you: a spice jar, coffee, a slice of orange peel, a bar of soap. Hold it close and breathe it in slowly, a few times, the way the spice box goes around.
Then set it down, rest your hands, and let the smell fade on its own. Nothing to finish.

wordCard.voice: A day off: in the Jewish Shabbat, a day when the work is put down because the day has come, finished or not.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shabbat, the seventh day of rest, kept from Friday sunset to Saturday night.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: rest arrives on time, and you may regard the work as done, finished or not.

sources.q: and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.
